content.paragraph: The method we used to sketch curves in the preceding section was a culmination of much of our study of differential calculus. The graph was the final object that we produced. In this section our point of view is completely different. Here we start with a graph produced by a graphing calculator or computer and then we refine it. We use calculus to make sure that we reveal all the important aspects of the curve. And with the use of graphing devices we can tackle curves that would be far too complicated to consider without technology. The theme is the interaction between calculus and technology.

problem.paragraph: Graph the polynomial $$f(x) = 2x^{6} + 3x^{5} + 3x^{3} - 2x^{2}$$ . Use the graphs of $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$f^{''}$$ to estimate all maximum and minimum points and intervals of concavity.

Solution If we specify a domain but not a range, graphing software will often deduce a suitable range from the values computed. Figure 1 shows a plot that may result if we specify that $$- 5 \leqslant x \leqslant 5$$ . Although this viewing rectangle is useful for showing that the asymptotic behavior (or end behavior) is the same as for $$y = 2x^{6}$$ , it is obviously hiding some finer detail. So we change to the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {- 3,2} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 50,100} \right\rbrack$$ in Figure 2.

The curve y = f(x) enters the viewing window at approximately (negative 5, 19,000), goes down and to the right, concave up, briefly flattens near the origin, and then goes up and to the right, and exits the viewing window at approximately (5, 40,000).

A curve is graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis is displayed from negative 3 to 2 in increments of 1 unit. The vertical axis is displayed from negative 50 to 100 in increments of 50 units. The curve y = f(x) enters the viewing window at approximately (negative 2.5, 100), goes down and to the right, concave up, crosses the x axis at (negative 2, 0), reaches its low point at approximately (negative 1.6, negative 20), then goes up and to the right, and inflects at approximately (negative 1.2, negative 10). After inflection, the curve then rises, now concave down, briefly flattens near the origin where it inflects again, then goes up and to the right in the first quadrant, now concave up, and exits the viewing window at approximately (1.8, 100).

problem.paragraph: Most graphing calculators and graphing software allow us to “trace” along a curve and see approximate coordinates of points. (Some also have features to identify the approximate locations of local maximum and minimum points.) Here it appears that there is an absolute minimum value of about $$- 15.33$$ when $$x \approx - 1.62$$ and $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1.62} \right)$$ and increasing on $$\left( {- 1.62,\infty} \right)$$ . Also, there appears to be a horizontal tangent at the origin and inflection points when $$x = 0$$ and when $$x$$ is somewhere between $$- 2$$ and $$- 1$$ .
Now let’s try to confirm these impressions using calculus. We differentiate and get

When we graph $$f^{\prime}$$ in Figure 3 we see that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from negative to positive when $$x \approx - 1.62$$ ; this confirms (by the First Derivative Test) the minimum value that we found earlier. But, perhaps to our surprise, we also notice that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from positive to negative when $$x = 0$$ and from negative to positive when $$x \approx 0.35$$ . This means that $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$0$$ and a local minimum when $$x \approx 0.35$$ , but these were hidden in Figure 2. Indeed, if we now zoom in toward the origin in Figure 4, we see what we missed before: a local maximum value of $$0$$ when $$x = 0$$ and a local minimum value of about $$- 0.1$$ when $$x \approx 0.35$$ .

After inflection, the curve then goes down and to the right through the origin, now concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (0.2, negative 1), then goes up and to the right, and exits the viewing window at approximately (1, 20).

The curve y = f(x) enters the viewing window at approximately (negative 0.5, negative 1), goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point at the origin, then goes down and to the right, inflects at approximately (0.2, negative 0.2). After inflection, the curve then goes down and to the right, now concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (0.4, negative 0.3), then goes up and to the right by crossing the x axis at (0.5, 0), and exits the viewing window at approximately (0.6, 1).

problem.paragraph: What about concavity and inflection points? From Figures 2, and 4 there appear to be inflection points when $$x$$ is a little to the left of $$- 1$$ and when $$x$$ is a little to the right of $$0$$ . But it’s difficult to determine inflection points from the graph of $$f$$ , so we graph the second derivative $$f^{''}$$ in Figure 5. We see that $$f^{''}$$ changes from positive to negative when $$x \approx - 1.23$$ and from negative to positive when $$x \approx 0.19$$ . So, correct to two decimal places, $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1.23} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0.19,\infty} \right)$$ and concave downward on $$\left( {- 1.23,0.19} \right)$$ . The inflection points are $$\left( {- 1.23, - 10.18} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0.19, - 0.05} \right)$$ .

The vertical axis is displayed from negative 30 to 10 in increments of 10 units. The curve y = f prime prime (x) enters the viewing window at approximately (negative 1.2, 10), goes down and to the right, crosses the x axis at approximately (negative 1.2, 0), concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (negative 0.8, negative 24), then goes up and to the right, and inflects at approximately (negative 0.6, negative 20). After inflection, the curve then goes up and to the right, now concave down until (0, negative 4), then goes up and to the right through (0.19, 0), becoming concave up again, and exits the viewing window at approximately (0.4, 10).

problem.paragraph: We have discovered that no single graph reveals all the important features of this polynomial. But Figures 2, and 4, when taken together, do provide an accurate picture.
Draw the graph of the function

in a viewing rectangle that shows all the important features of the function. Estimate the local maximum and minimum values and the intervals of concavity. Then use calculus to find these quantities exactly.

Solution Figure 6—produced by graphing software with automatic scaling—is a disaster. Some graphing calculators use $$\left\lbrack {- 10,10} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 10,10} \right\rbrack$$ as the default viewing rectangle, so let’s try it. We get the graph shown in Figure 7; it’s a major improvement.

figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis is displayed from negative 5 to 5. The vertical axis is displayed from 0 to 3 times 10^8. The curve y = f(x) has two parts. The first part appears to run rightward along the negative horizontal axis in the given viewing rectangle, then gradually goes down and to the right, becoming concave up, reaches its low point in the third quadrant very close to the x axis, then rises steeply to the right in the second quadrant very close to the vertical axis, and appears to reach a sharp point on the vertical axis in this viewing rectangle. The second part enters the first quadrant at the top, near the vertical axis, appears to fall to the right from the sharp point, concave up, veers toward the horizontal axis, running almost along with it, exiting near the right extreme.

A curve is graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal and the vertical axes are displayed from negative 10 to 10. The curve y = f(x) has two parts. The first part enters the second quadrant very close to and above the horizontal axis, goes down and to the right, concave down, inflects at approximately (negative 3, negative 3), goes down and to the right, now concave up, and reaches its low point at (negative 1, negative 3.5). It then goes up and to the right by crossing the negative x axis, approaches the vertical axis, and exits the second quadrant very close to and to the left of it. The second part lies entirely in the first quadrant. It enters to the right of the vertical axis, goes down and to the right, concave up, and runs almost parallel to the horizontal axis as the curve proceeds rightward.

problem.paragraph: The $$y$$-axis appears to be a vertical asymptote and indeed it is because

Figure 7 also allows us to estimate the $$x$$-intercepts: about $$- 0.5$$ and $$- 6.5$$ . The exact values are obtained by using the quadratic formula to solve the equation $$x^{2} + 7x + 3 = 0$$ ; we get $$x = {({- 7 \pm \sqrt{37}})} \slash 2$$ .

To get a better look at horizontal asymptotes, we change to the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {- 20,20} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 5,10} \right\rbrack$$ in Figure 8. It appears that $$y = 1$$ is the horizontal asymptote and this is easily confirmed:

It then rises steeply to the right, veering toward the vertical axis, approaching it very close to and to the left of the vertical axis. The second part enters the first quadrant at approximately (1, 10), goes down and to the right, concave up, veers toward the horizontal line y = 1, and exits very closely above it.

problem.paragraph: To estimate the minimum value we zoom in to the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {- 3,0} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 4,2} \right\rbrack$$ in Figure 9. We find that the absolute minimum value is about $$- 3.1$$ when $$x \approx - 0.9$$ , and we see that the function decreases on $$\left( {- \infty, - 0.9} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ and increases on $$\left( {- 0.9,0} \right)$$ . The exact values are obtained by differentiating:

The vertical axis is displayed from negative 4 to 2 in increments of 2 units. The curve y = f(x) enters the viewing window in the third quadrant at approximately (negative 3, negative 1), goes down and to the right, concave down, inflects at approximately (negative 1.2, negative 2.75), then goes down and to the right, now concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (negative 0.8, negative 3.08), then goes up and to the right, crosses the x axis at approximately (negative 0.5, 0), and exits the viewing window at approximately (negative 0.4, 2).

problem.paragraph: This shows that $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$- \frac{6}{7} < x < 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ when $$x < - \frac{6}{7}$$ and when $$x > 0$$ . The exact minimum value is $$f\left( {- \frac{6}{7}} \right) = - \frac{37}{12} \approx - 3.08$$ .

Figure 9 also shows that an inflection point occurs somewhere between $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = - 2$$ . We could estimate it much more accurately using the graph of the second derivative, but in this case it’s just as easy to find exact values. Since

we see that $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ when $$x > - \frac{9}{7}\left( {x \neq 0} \right)$$ and $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ when $$x < - \frac{9}{7}$$ . So $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {- \frac{9}{7},0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ and concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty, - \frac{9}{7}} \right)$$ . The inflection point is $$\left( {- \frac{9}{7}, - \frac{71}{27}} \right)$$ .
The analysis using the first two derivatives shows that Figure 8 displays all the major aspects of the curve.
Graph the function $$f(x) = \frac{x^{2}\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}}{\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2}\left( {x - 4} \right)^{4}}$$ .

Solution Drawing on our experience with a rational function in Example 2, let’s start by graphing $$f$$ in the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {- 10,10} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 10,10} \right\rbrack$$ . From Figure 10 we have the feeling that we are going to have to zoom in to see some finer detail and also zoom out to see the larger picture. But, as a guide to intelligent zooming, let’s first take a close look at the expression for $$f(x)$$ . Because of the factors $$\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2}$$ and $$\left( {x - 4} \right)^{4}$$ in the denominator, we expect $$x = 2$$ and $$x = 4$$ to be the vertical asymptotes. Indeed
and

The curve y = f(x) appears to run along the negative horizontal axis in this viewing window, passes through the origin, then goes up and to the right in the first quadrant, concave up, rising almost parallel to the vertical axis, and exits the viewing window at approximately (1.5, 10). The second part enters the first quadrant at approximately (8, 10), goes down and to the right, concave up, and exits the viewing window at approximately (10, 2).

problem.paragraph: To find the horizontal asymptotes, we divide numerator and denominator by $$x^{6}$$ :
This shows that $$\left. f(x)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow \pm \infty \right.$$ , so the $$x$$-axis is a horizontal asymptote.

It is also very useful to consider the behavior of the graph near the $$x$$-intercepts using an analysis like that in Example 2.6.12. Since $$x^{2}$$ is positive, $$f(x)$$ does not change sign at $$0$$ and so its graph doesn’t cross the $$x$$-axis at $$0$$ . But, because of the factor $$\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}$$ , the graph does cross the $$x$$-axis at $$- 1$$ and has a horizontal tangent there. Putting all this information together, but without using derivatives, we see that the curve has to look something like the one in Figure 11.

figure.alt_text: Two dashed vertical lines and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from below negative 1 to beyond 4 in increments of 1 unit. Two dashed vertical lines extend upward in the first quadrant from (2, 0) and (4, 0). The curve has three parts. The first part enters the third quadrant below the x axis, goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches its low point at approximately x = negative 1.3, then goes up and to the right, briefly levels out at (negative 1, 0) where it inflects. It then goes up and to the right, reaches its high point at approximately x = negative 0.4, goes down and to the right, reaches its low point at the origin, and then goes up and to the right in the first quadrant, veering toward x = 2, approaches it. The second part resembles a U-shaped curve and lies between x = 2 and x = 4. It enters to the right of x = 2 at the top, goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches its low point at x = 3, then goes up and to the right, approaches x = 4. The third part enters to the right of x = 4, goes down, and to the right, concave up, veering away from x = 4, and exits the viewing window above the x axis.

problem.paragraph: We can read from these graphs that the absolute minimum is about $$- 0.02$$ and occurs when $$x \approx - 20$$ . There is also a local maximum $$\approx 0.00002$$ when $$x \approx - 0.3$$ and a local minimum $$\approx 211$$ when $$x \approx 2.5$$ . These graphs also show three inflection points near $$- 35$$ , $$- 5$$ , and $$- 1$$ and two between $$- 1$$ and $$0$$ . To estimate the inflection points closely we would need to graph $$f^{''}$$ , but to compute $$f^{''}$$ by hand is an unreasonable chore. If you have a computer algebra system, then it’s easy to do (see Exercise 15).

We have seen that, for this particular function, three graphs (Figures 12, 13, and 14) are necessary to convey all the useful information. The only way to display all these features of the function on a single graph is to draw it by hand. Despite the exaggerations and distortions, Figure 11 does manage to summarize the essential nature of the function.

Graph the function $$f(x) = \sin\left( {x + \sin 2x} \right)$$ . For $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant \pi$$ , estimate all maximum and minimum values, intervals of increase and decrease, and inflection points.

Solution We first note that $$f$$ is periodic with period $$2\pi$$ . Also, $$f$$ is odd and $$\left| {f(x)} \right| \leqslant 1$$ for all $$x$$ . So the choice of a viewing rectangle is not a problem for this function: we start with $$\left\lbrack {0,\pi} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 1.1,1.1} \right\rbrack$$ . (See Figure 15.) It appears that there are three local maximum values and two local minimum values in that window. To confirm these values and locate them more accurately, we calculate that
and graph both $$f$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ in Figure 16.

content.paragraph: Our final example is concerned with families of functions. This means that the functions in the family are related to each other by a formula that contains one or more arbitrary constants. Each value of the constant gives rise to a member of the family and the idea is to see how the graph of the function changes as the constant changes.

problem.paragraph: How does the graph of $$f(x) = 1 \slash \left( {x^{2} + 2x + c} \right)$$ vary as $$c$$ varies?
Solution The graphs in Figures 19 and 20 (the special cases $$c = 2$$ and $$c = - 2$$ ) show two very different-looking curves.

problem.paragraph: Before drawing any more graphs, let’s see what members of this family have in common. Since

for any value of $$c$$ , they all have the $$x$$-axis as a horizontal asymptote. A vertical asymptote will occur when $$x^{2} + 2x + c = 0$$ . Solving this quadratic equation, we get $$x = - 1 \pm \sqrt{1 - c}$$ . When $$c > 1$$ , there is no vertical asymptote (as in Figure 19). When $$c = 1$$ , the graph has a single vertical asymptote $$x = - 1$$ because
When $$c < 1$$ , there are two vertical asymptotes: $$x = - 1 \pm \sqrt{1 - c}$$ (as in Figure 20).
Now we compute the derivative:

This shows that $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$x = - 1$$ (if $$c \neq 1$$ ), $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$x < - 1$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ when $$x > - 1$$ . For $$c \geqslant 1$$ , this means that $$f$$ increases on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ and decreases on $$\left( {- 1,\infty} \right)$$ . For $$c > 1$$ , there is an absolute maximum value $$f\left( {- 1} \right) = 1 \slash \left( {c - 1} \right)$$ . For $$c < 1$$ , $$f\left( {- 1} \right) = 1 \slash \left( {c - 1} \right)$$ is a local maximum value and the intervals of increase and decrease are interrupted at the vertical asymptotes.

Figure 21 is a “slide show” displaying five members of the family, all graphed in the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {- 5,4} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 2,2} \right\rbrack$$ . As predicted, a transition takes place from two vertical asymptotes to one for $$c = 1$$ , and then to none for $$c > 1$$ . As $$c$$ increases from $$1$$ , we see that the maximum point becomes lower; this is explained by the fact that $$\left. 1 \slash \left( {c - 1} \right)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. c\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . As $$c$$ decreases from $$1$$ , the vertical asymptotes become more widely separated because the distance between them is $$2\sqrt{1 - c}$$ , which becomes large as $$\left. c\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ . Again, the maximum point approaches the $$x$$-axis because $$\left. 1 \slash \left( {c - 1} \right)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. c\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ .

The first outermost curve enters the second quadrant, goes down and to the right, concave up, crosses the x axis at approximately (negative 1.9, 0), reaches its low point at approximately (negative 1.4, negative 3), then goes up and to the right through the approximate point (negative 0.5, 0), now concave down, reaches its high point at (0, 1). It then goes down and to the right through the approximate point (0.5, 0), now concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (1.4, negative 3), and then goes up and to the right through the approximate point (1.9, 0), mirroring its earlier path. The second curve enters to the right of the first curve, goes down and to the right through the approximate point (negative 1.3, 0), reaches its low point at (negative 1, negative 1), then rises to a high point at (0, 1), goes down and to the right, reaches its low point at (1, negative 1), then rises through the approximate point (1.3, 0) into the first quadrant, and exits to the left of the first curve. As we move from the outermost first curve to the innermost seventh curve, the curve becomes steeper and the low points of the curves become closer to the y axis. A red downward opening parabola, enters the third quadrant at the bottom left, goes up and to the right through the low points of the seven W-shaped curves to the left of the y axis, reaches its high point at (0, 1), and then goes down and to the right through the low points of the seven curves, to the right of the y axis. Four blue downward opening parabolas enter the third quadrant to the right of the red parabola, reach its vertex at (0, 1), and exit the fourth quadrant to the left of the red parabola.
